## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet, and scores stay hidden, so this round is a spread of reasoned bets. Under the default recipe the budget is only about 32 PPO updates (131k steps ÷ 4,096 per update). So each update has to count, and a stronger built-in structure should matter more than a bigger network. Any network costing more compute than the starting one gets fewer training steps, so all candidates stay at or below its cost (r ≤ 1). On this task a placement is right only when the brick's landing layer (the highest filled cell under it) is filled in the target and missing in the build for every cell it covers, and no missing target cells get sealed underneath. The starting head pools one mixed feature vector per cell, which makes these per-layer checks hard to learn. I propose a per-layer footprint head that pools features for each layer separately over the brick footprint, and a recipe that doubles the number of updates. Together with the starting network this forms a 2x2 test, run as three trials.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials trained without errors, but scores are hidden, so we can't tell which design or recipe is ahead. I have to reason from the task itself. A placement is correct only if three things hold. The brick lands at layer L, the highest build height under its footprint. The target contains every footprint cell at layer L. And under the footprint, the build already matches the target up to L, so no gap gets sealed. Per-layer features are the natural way to represent this. However, r1c1/r1c3 mix all layers through one 1x1 conv that has separate weights for each layer, so each layer's rule is learned separately. A scorer whose weights are shared across layers would let every layer's data train one rule, then pick the landing layer with a soft max over layers. I test that scorer with both recipes. I also test fewer PPO epochs (more samples and updates) on the r1c1 network to learn whether sample count or reuse limits learning.

### Round 3
All six trials trained without errors, but no scores are shown, so I can't rank them. The search has covered three structures: the starting network, a per-layer footprint head and a layer-shared logsumexp scorer. It has also covered two recipe directions: more frequent updates (128 envs, gamma 0.97, lambda 0.92) and 2 PPO epochs, which nearly doubles the training samples. With feedback hidden, the best use of the last trials is to spread across options that are each plausible but not yet tried. Two gaps stand out. The layer-shared scorer and the starting network have never been trained with the 2-epoch, more-samples recipe. That recipe should help generalisation to held-out designs because the agent sees more distinct designs. Also, no placement head has yet seen global context about overall build progress, which matters for placement order and overhangs. Each new candidate stays well inside the time limit: r2c3 ran 241k steps without a problem.

### Round 4
No scores are visible. Every trial trained cleanly, so nothing here can be ranked on evidence; only reasoning separates them. Three things should help. First, the per-layer footprint features fit the drop rule. Second, fewer PPO epochs buy more fresh designs (2 epochs gives about 1.8x the samples) and more updates, which should help on held-out designs. Third, build-wide context should help with placement order. r3c3 combines all three. Its 1.17x compute keeps it fast, so it is the base for this round. As this is the last round, I chose three candidates that differ in kind so the final selection has distinct options: (a) push the sample-count idea to 1 epoch; (b) use a longer reward horizon for the exact-build bonus, plus less entropy so greedy play is sharper; (c) feed the legality mask and the layer above each cell into the network, so it can see overhang and height-limit structure.
